page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The products
lines: Boron trifluoride BF₃ reacts with lithium
Each fluorine on boron is replaced by
hydrogen, and two BH₃ units join as B₂H₆.
steps.why: LiH supplies hydride, H⁻, and BF₃ supplies boron. Every B–F bond is swapped for a B–H bond, and because BH₃ is not stable on its own the two boron atoms join as the dimer B₂H₆. The fluorine leaves with lithium as LiF.
common_mistakes: Writing BH₃ as the boron product. BH₃ is not stable on its own, so the product is the dimer B₂H₆.
Leaving out LiF. Every fluorine atom on the left must also appear on the right, and the fluorine leaves as lithium fluoride.
steps.memory_tip: Swap every F for an H, then pair the two BH₃ units into B₂H₆.
steps.margin_note: Name both products in words as well as in formulas.

steps.label: The balanced equation
lines: Balance boron first, then fluorine and
steps.why: One B₂H₆ needs two boron atoms, so the equation starts with 2BF₃. Those two BF₃ molecules carry six fluorine atoms, which need six lithium atoms to leave as 6LiF, and the six hydrogen atoms of B₂H₆ come from the same six LiH.
common_mistakes: Writing BF₃ + LiH → B₂H₆ + LiF with no coefficients. The atom counts on the two sides do not match.
Using 3LiH instead of 6LiH. Six hydrogen atoms are needed to build one B₂H₆.
steps.memory_tip: Two borons in B₂H₆ fixes 2BF₃, and six hydrogens fixes 6LiH.
steps.margin_note: Write the atom count under the equation to show it balances.

insider_note: The balanced equation is the whole answer here, so write the coefficients the first time and put the atom count beneath it.
